drafts.subject: Re: Prospective GSoC contributor - where to start?
drafts.message:
Hi Fatima,

Thanks so much for reaching out — it's great to hear from a Waterloo student who's already diving into Jac! We love seeing enthusiastic contributors get involved early, and your Python background is a perfect foundation for working with Jaseci.

Here are a few suggestions to help you get started:

**Repositories to explore:**
- **jaseci** — the core runtime and compiler for the Jac language. This is where most of the language-level work happens, and it's a great place to get familiar with the internals.
- **jaseci-python** — Python bindings and toolkit integrations. Since you're already comfortable with Python, this is probably your most natural entry point.
- **jaseci-contrib** — community-contributed modules and kits. Good-first-issues here tend to be more self-contained and beginner-friendly.

**How to begin:**
1. Head over to our GitHub organization (github.com/Jaseci-Labs) and browse the repos listed above.
2. Look for issues tagged **"good first issue"** or **"help wanted"** — these are curated for newcomers and usually come with enough context to get going without deep prior knowledge.
3. Clone a repo, get it building locally, and try running through some of the examples in the docs you've already been reading.
4. When you find an issue that interests you, drop a comment saying you'd like to work on it, and we'll help you get unblocked.

**Getting ready for GSoC:**
- Start contributing now — even small PRs (docs fixes, test improvements, minor bug fixes) count. A track record of merged PRs makes a huge difference when GSoC applications open.
- Join our community channel (you'll find the link in the repo READMEs) — that's where mentors hang out and where we post project ideas as GSoC season approaches.
- Keep an eye out for our GSoC project ideas list, which we typically publish early in the year. Having prior contributions to the project you apply for strengthens your proposal significantly.

Since you've already been learning Jac from the docs, you're ahead of the curve. If you run into any roadblocks — whether it's setting up the dev environment, understanding a piece of the architecture, or just figuring out where to look — don't hesitate to ask. We're happy to help.

Looking forward to your first PR!

Best,
The Jaseci Team

drafts.subject: Re: Bug: edge traversal returns duplicates after node delete (repro attached)
drafts.message:
Hi Omar,

Thanks for the detailed report — this is a great repro and very much appreciated.

To answer your questions:

1. Known issue: Yes, this is a known issue in Jac 0.10.2. After a node is deleted, stale edge references can remain in the adjacency structures of its former neighbors, so a [-->] traversal may surface duplicate or dangling edge entries. The underlying problem is that edge cleanup on node deletion doesn't fully flush the neighbor-side edge lists in all cases.

2. Workaround: While the fix is being finalized, you can work around this by filtering traversed edges for validity. After traversing from a node, check that each returned edge's source and target still resolve to non-deleted nodes before acting on it. A simple dedup pass (e.g., tracking seen edge IDs) will also eliminate the duplicates. This should be safe to ship in production.

3. GitHub issue: Absolutely — please do file one with your full reproduction snippet. Having the minimal repro (nodes A, B, C with edges A->B, B->C; delete B; traverse from A) in the issue will help us attach it directly to the fix PR and verify the resolution. Link the issue back here if you can.

We're targeting the fix for the next patch release. I'll follow up on the GitHub issue once the PR is up so you can test against it.

Thanks again for catching this and for the offer to help — it makes a real difference.

Best,
The Jaseci Team

drafts.subject: Re: Press: quote on agentic programming languages (deadline Aug 5 EOD)
drafts.message:
Hi Grace,

Thanks for reaching out — happy to contribute to your piece. Here's a quote you can use:

"General-purpose programming languages were built around deterministic control flow and human-authored logic, so building agentic software with them means bolting on layers of orchestration, memory management, and reasoning through external frameworks. Agent-native languages like Jaseci instead treat autonomous actors, their cognitive state, and inter-agent communication as first-class primitives — letting developers express agentic behavior directly and at a fraction of the code, without sacrificing flexibility or performance."

Feel free to attribute this to the Jaseci team. Let me know if you need anything else before your deadline.

Best,
The Jaseci Team
